1:
Luke opens the chapter with a scene rather than a saying, and the commentators read the scene closely. Gill places it on a sabbath, and has the crowd close in on Jesus as he comes out of the Pharisee’s house where he had been at dinner — they could not get near him while he was inside. Ellicott builds the same connection from the Greek: the tense is continuous, and all the publicans and the sinners were drawing near to hear Him, and what emboldened them was that they had just seen Jesus turn, as in indignation, from that Pharisee’s table. Robertson confirms the grammar. The verb is a periphrastic imperfect, a drawing-near that went on; the infinitive to hear is a present of purpose; and the doubled article separates two classes rather than lumping them, all the publicans and the sinners, so that the tax-farmers are placed on the same footing as the openly disreputable.

Who the sinners were is disputed. Clarke takes the pair as tax-gatherers and heathens, people who believed neither in Christ nor in Moses. Wesley and Henry both suspect a Gentile setting, Wesley reading all as all who were in that place and locating Jesus in some town of Galilee of the Gentiles. Henry adds that the publicans were not necessarily bad men but were industriously put into an ill name because of the national grudge against their office, and he notices the modesty of the approach: they came near enough to hear and no nearer, and they came not to ask for cures but for the teaching.

The murmur is examined with the same care. Robertson takes the compound verb to mean grumbling passed among themselves, a word used only twice in the New Testament, and reads the demonstrative this man as an open sneer, probably with a pointing finger. The verb translated receiveth he renders as giving a person access to oneself, welcoming, the same word used of Martha; the present tense makes it a settled habit, and the charge of eating with them is the graver breach, an old accusation already made in the fifth chapter. Clarke presses the same verb warmly: he receives them cordially, takes them to his bosom. Barnes reads the logic of the slander — kindness was treated as evidence of shared character — and answers that the very object of Christ’s coming was to call the wicked from their ways. Henry notes that the objectors could not for shame attack the preaching, so they attacked the meal, which at least broke the tradition of the elders.

Two older voices supply the frame. Ambrose reads the chapter as the remedy offered after the fall, the good Physician showing a cure to those who could not keep a firm step in so slippery a world, and the merciful Judge not denying the hope of pardon. Gregory turns the mirror on the objectors: true justice feels compassion, false justice scorn; the just rebuke sinners out of zeal for discipline while inwardly setting them above themselves, whereas those who think themselves no sinners are so much the worse sinners. Of such, he says, were these men, who in condemning the reception of sinners reviled the very fountain of mercy.
3:
Gill reads the parable as aimed three ways at once: at the Pharisees for conviction, at the publicans for encouragement, and at the vindication of the speaker himself. Wesley makes the same point of all three parables together — sheep, coin and son declare, in direct contrariety to the scribes, in what manner God receives sinners. Robertson calls it Christ’s way of answering chronic complainers, notes that the same story serves a different purpose in Matthew, and quotes with approval a scheme of the trilogy as a climb: the pasture, the house, the home; the herdsman, the housewife, the father; the sheep, the treasure, the beloved son.

The details of the picture draw close attention. Robertson insists the wilderness is the flock’s ordinary pasturage and not a place of peril, that the participle for lost is intransitive, and that the shepherd keeps on going, a linear present, until an effective aorist brings success. Wesley agrees on the ground: any uncultivated land, like an English common, the Jews called wilderness. Lightfoot documents the round number, showing that dividing between one and ninety-nine was a familiar Jewish habit, and cites the saying that of the hundred cries a woman in travail utters, ninety-nine are to death and one to life. Clarke, who notes that similar parables are common in Jewish writers, presses the natural history: no creature strays more easily or is less able to find its way back, for it will bleat for the flock and still run in the opposite direction, which he says he has often watched. He adds that ravens pick out lambs’ eyes so that the blinded creature stumbles into ruin, as Satan blinds the understanding, and asks who but a Pharisee or a devil would fault a shepherd for the rescue.

What the ninety-nine represent is genuinely contested. Clarke takes the flock as all mankind, Jew and Gentile alike, belonging to its divine owner. Ellicott, reading the parable against the Good Shepherd discourse, allows the primary sense to be the love that concentrates on one soul among the publicans then present, but extends it to the whole redemptive work, the ninety-nine being unfallen angels or possibly unfallen beings in other worlds. Gregory reads them the same way and sharpens it: the hundred was complete when angels and men together stood, and the shepherd left the companies of angels in heaven because it was on earth that the number had been broken. Cyril presses the arithmetic — a hundred is perfect, being ten decades — and answers the obvious objection, that the shepherd was not angry with the rest but left them in safety, since only the perishing needed pity and only their return would restore the figure. Augustine breaks with all of these, taking the ninety-nine left in the wilderness for the proud, who carry a solitude about in their minds because they wish to appear alone, and who lack the one thing that would make them complete.

On the carrying home the readings converge. Ellicott sees a threefold parallel: Christ bearing the weak sheep, Christ bearing our nature and its infirmities, and disciples following in the same steps. Gregory of Nyssa notes that the shepherd neither punished the sheep nor drove it back but lifted it and carried it gently. Gregory adds that the shoulders are the assumed manhood under the weight of our sins, and that the friends and neighbours are the angelic companies; he lingers on the wording, that the call is not to rejoice with the sheep but with me. Robertson finds the same instinct in the grammar, a verb of mutual joy: joy demands fellowship. Ambrose puts it shortest — rich indeed is that shepherd of whom we are all a hundredth part.
7:
The verse turns on a phrase nobody is comfortable with, and the readings of just persons, which need no repentance divide sharply. Barnes begins by removing a word: persons is not in the Greek, which says only just ones, and the term may cover angels as easily as men. He denies flatly that any just men exist on earth who need no repentance, citing Ecclesiastes, the Psalms and Romans, and argues that the saying describes what happens in heaven, among beings who watch the creatures of God and rejoice more at one recovery than at many who never fell. He warns against arithmetic: the ratio is not ninety-nine unfallen to one lost, and the point is comparative feeling, not census. Clarke takes the opposite tack and lets the phrase stand of real people — those raised sober and regular, honest in their dealings, who differ both from the heathen and from the tax-gatherers of the opening verses and who cannot repent of crimes they never committed. Such men, he says, are in no danger, and God will make further discoveries of his holiness to them as he did to Cornelius. Clarke then reports, without rejecting it, the older opinion that the ninety-nine are angels, standing to men as ninety-nine to one, so that the incarnation took human and not angelic nature.

Ellicott will have none of this. He reads the words as a grave and indignant protest veiled as a concession, aimed at Pharisaic self-satisfaction: the call to repent had gone out to all, and that every man offends in many things was the first postulate of every gospel preacher, whatever his school. He finds the opposite sentiment only once, in the penitent’s prayer that God appointed no repentance for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and there it comes wrapped in confession by a man who felt how unlike those saints he was. It was left to the Pharisees to turn the thought into a settled conviction. Robertson reaches the same place by grammar: there is no comparative in the Greek at all, only an idiom like our rather than, and Jesus is accepting the objectors’ claims about themselves for the sake of argument in order to condemn them out of their own mouths, exactly as he had done at the tax-collector’s feast.

Lightfoot supplies the background the others assume, showing from the Jewish schools that just persons was simply the standing name for the good who would finally be saved, set against the wicked, and he amuses himself with the rabbinic play on the bent and the upright forms of the letter Tsadi, which was taken to mean that the upright man must first be bowed down.

On the joy itself there is agreement. Gill allows the heaven in view to be either the church below, which the Apocalypse can call heaven, or heaven above among the angels. Wesley makes it solemn and festal joy, first in Christ himself and then among the angels and the spirits of just men, who may be informed of it by God or by the ministering angels; the sinner is the gross and notorious one, and the repentance a thorough change of heart and life. Tertullian grounds the rejoicing in ownership: the one who sought was the one who lost, and the one who lost was the one who owned, so the gladness belongs to the Creator who declared long before that he would rather the sinner repent than die. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the verse on his hearers — make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, he tells the newly enrolled, that there may be gladness among the inhabitants of heaven.
8:
The second parable is read as a deliberate variation rather than a repetition. Chrysostom sets the two side by side: the sheep showed that we are creatures of the God who made us, the coin that we were struck with the royal likeness, for a coin is metal bearing the king’s image. Ellicott reaches the same point independently and adds two more differences. The coin is lost inside the house, which allows that a soul precious to God may be lost within Israel or within the visible church; and it is a woman who searches, which he refuses to explain away as a bid for the interest of the women listening. The graces required for recovering the fallen — patience, diligence, minute observation — are the ones usually called feminine, and are needed no less than courage and enterprise. In the woman he sees partly the Wisdom of Proverbs, partly the church.

Who the woman is divides the readers. Gill makes her Christ, the ten coins the whole Jewish nation once a peculiar treasure and now reprobate silver, and the nine the scribes and Pharisees; he presses the image hard, since a lost coin contributes nothing whatever to its own finding, which is his proof of the sinner’s passivity in conversion. Gregory makes her God and the wisdom of God, and reads the nine as the nine orders of angels, man being created tenth to fill the number of the elect. Augustine again dissents, taking the nine exactly as he took the ninety-nine, for those who trust themselves and prefer themselves to sinners coming back. Gregory of Nyssa moves the whole picture inside a single soul: the coins are the several virtues, and their possession profits nothing while the one is missing that carries the divine image; the candle is the word that brings hidden things to light, or the torch of repentance; the house is a man’s own conscience; the image is not defaced but buried under dirt, and shines out when a well-spent life wipes it away.

The particulars are worked over closely. Robertson notes the only occurrence of the word in the New Testament, traces it to a verb meaning to grasp, so that the sum is a handful of coin worth about a quarter of a shekel, calls the verb for sweeping a late colloquial form, and infers a windowless house with a dirt floor, which is why a lamp is lit by day. He also catches a difference the others miss: she lost the coin, whereas the shepherd did not lose the sheep. Gill and Barnes both reckon the value in English money, Barnes adding it was all she had. Clarke prefers to keep the ancient names: a longer a coin lies lost the less likely it is to be found, since it loses its colour, gathers dirt, and may have the image and superscription worn off it altogether — then warns that parables must not be made to go on all fours. Lightfoot produces a rabbinic parallel in which a man who loses a shekel lights candles and torches until he finds it, and argues from the lesser to the greater.

On the closing verse Gregory Nazianzen has the finder make the heavenly powers partners in the joy, and Theophylact distinguishes the friends, who do his will, from the neighbours who stand nearest — thrones, cherubim, seraphim. Robertson reads the present tense as joy arising, and takes joy in the presence of the angels to mean the joy of God himself, the angels being in a sense his neighbours. Calvin asks the hard question directly: why should one conversion outweigh long perseverance? Because God’s mercy shines more brightly in rescuing one already cut off as a rotten member, and Scripture ascribes to him, after the manner of men, the gladness of an unexpected good.
11:
Ambrose reads the three parables as one prescription: Christ the shepherd carries you, the church as the woman searches, God as father receives — pity, intercession, reconciliation. Chrysostom sharpens the difference: the shepherd seeks a sheep that cannot find its way back, which is why the man taken in by another’s guile is likened to an irrational animal, while the father receives a son exercising his own will. Calvin calls it a confirmation of the doctrine already given, the first half showing how readily God pardons, the second the malignity of those who resent it, with a father who does not merely forgive on request but goes out to meet.

The identification of the two sons is the chapter’s largest dispute. Barnes and Henry take the obvious reading, the younger for the publicans and sinners, the elder for the scribes and Pharisees, and Gill agrees, observing that man as sinner is younger than man as righteous and that God has chosen the younger before the elder before now. Henry adds that God is here Father to the whole family of Adam, so that the despised publicans are the Pharisees’ own brethren, and draws the pair as characters: one grave and austere, sober but sour to those around him, the other volatile and impatient of restraint. Wesley reads the request itself as the root of all sin, a desire to dispose of ourselves independently of God. Lightfoot notes that reading the elder as the Jew and the younger as the Gentile is no novelty, and that it suits the boast of never having transgressed and the fury at a brother’s reception, since nothing was more grievous to that nation than the welcome of the Gentiles. Ellicott holds both together, the narrower application to Pharisees and publicans and the wider one to Israel and the heathen world, traced to the lines of Shem and Japheth; but he turns the parable against a reading he had allowed earlier, arguing that since the elder son plainly cannot stand for the unfallen part of creation, this tells against taking the ninety-nine sheep or the nine coins for angels. Chrysostom had refused that reading on other ground: the younger son repented of his own accord, whereas mankind had to be called, and the elder resents what heaven rejoices over. Cyril reports the Israel-and-Gentiles reading but objects that a people so often reproved cannot say neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment, and prefers two ranks of one family: those righteous from the first, and those brought back by repentance. Augustine reads two nations from the beginning of the race, one that kept the worship of God and one that deserted to idols.

On the portion the commentators turn legal. Robertson cites the law of the double share, so that the younger’s half-portion is a third of the estate, normally payable at death,. Barnes agrees, suggests the younger took only movable property while the elder stayed on the land, and recalls that Roman and Syrophoenician custom let a son of age claim his share by law. Clarke presses this furthest, calling it an immemorial eastern custom that the father could not legally refuse, framed to protect a child from ill usage.

What the substance is gets a spiritual answer too. Cyril calls it the knowledge of good and evil, the reason given equally to everyone at birth and afterwards kept or squandered, and finds free will in the father’s refusal either to detain the one or to drive out the other. Theophylact makes it the capacity of reason with its liberty, and adds heaven, earth, the Law and the Prophets. Augustine has the soul, pleased with its own power, asking for what is properly God’s gift; Basil observes that age is a matter of mind and gravity rather than of grey hairs.
13:
Robertson tracks the two verbs against each other. The young man gathered together and then scattered — the second word is the one used of winnowing grain, the exact opposite of the first — and the verb for leaving home means he burned his bridges behind him. The adverb rendered riotous occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and comes from a root meaning unsaveable: a spendthrift, an abandoned man. Ellicott gives the same word as thriftless and fills in the scene from ordinary life, since emigration of this kind was familiar in the towns of Galilee and Judaea — a young man off to Alexandria or Rome or Corinth, and then the rumours coming home of money wasted, sabbaths broken, synagogues unvisited, perhaps even idol feasts. Beneath that he reads the far country as the state of a spirit wandering from God and the riotous living as noble gifts spent on sensuality or on idolatrous worship, with the first chapter of Romans as the fuller picture.

Barnes keeps to the surface: the property was converted into money, the journey undertaken for trade or fortune, and the phrase means living without saving anything, in dissolute company. Clarke supplies a motive the text does not — that the son hurried his departure for fear of the penalty and public reproach he would have incurred had the case gone before a magistrate — and, on the strength of the elder brother’s later charge, says the money went among harlots, the readiest way to exhaust the body and ruin the soul. Lightfoot takes up a question others pass by, whether this is the stubborn and rebellious son of Deuteronomy, and answers no on the authority of the Sanhedrin’s own definition, which is drawn so narrowly — he must steal from both parents, must eat and drink set quantities, must not have a lame or blind parent — that hardly such a son could exist.

The older readings are interior. Chrysostom insists the far country is not a place, since God is everywhere present, but the heart: the sinner flees in order to stand at a distance. Augustine traces the impulse to a perverse imitation, the wish to be governed by no one as God is governed by none, which ends in a soul grown cold and senseless and vanishing away from truth; and he defines the prodigal life as one that loves to spend and display itself outwardly while exhausting itself within, following whatever passes on and forsaking what is nearest. Ambrose reads the famine as a fast of the more wretched kind, not of food but of good works and virtues, since the man who leaves the word of God is hungry — man does not live by bread alone — and nothing satisfies a prodigal mind.

Wesley compresses both verses: far from God, God not in all his thoughts, all the grace he had received squandered, and the want felt when worldly pleasure failed. Gill draws his usual conclusion, that sin strips a man of the divine image and of strength for good, so that if he has spent all there is nothing left of free will, nothing to offer a creditor and no capacity to prepare himself for conversion. Barnes and Clarke both naturalise the famine, Barnes noting how common failures of crops and plague were in eastern lands and Clarke guessing that a man of that turn would have sought out a country of riot where want must follow. Ellicott recalls the famine under Claudius and turns the image inward, to the craving that appetite cannot fill and the famine that is not of bread but of hearing the word of the Lord.
15:
Robertson notes that the verb for joining is passive — a word for gluing, so that the man was stuck fast — and that citizen is a term found in the New Testament almost only in Luke. Ellicott presses the same verb further: it is the word used of a husband cleaving to his wife, and it marks the absolute dependence of a starving man on whoever will help him. On the surface the shame is that a son of Abraham had to live on an alien’s bounty; Barnes takes the citizen for a man of property who sent his hireling out of the city to the fields.

Who the citizen stands for is contested, and the disagreement is sharp. Wesley makes him the devil or one of his children, the genuine natives of a country far from God. Ambrose calls him a prince of the world and warns that the man who attaches himself is in a snare, with the sending to the farm meaning enslavement to worldly goods — Bede glosses the farm the same way, and finds the man sent to the estate who had excused himself from the kingdom. Augustine likewise names a prince of the air. Gill rejects both the saints and the devil: not the saints, since carnal men do not like their company; not the devil, who is no mere citizen of that country but its prince and god, and whom a man just beginning to feel his want would hardly seek out. He identifies instead an unregenerate legal preacher, since a man may have large gifts and a form of godliness without grace. Ellicott rules out the tempter for a different reason: the citizen is only one of many, and his part in the story is not to tempt but half-unconsciously to punish, and half-unconsciously to keep the offender alive so that rescue remains possible. He proposes instead worldly prudence and ethics without religion, which sustain a soul for a while, still the hungry edge of appetite, and leave it wretched.

On the swine there is no disagreement, only degrees of horror. Barnes calls it the deepest conceivable degradation for a Jew, since the animal was unclean to eat and therefore unlawful to keep, and takes the whole image as the measure of what sin does to what is noble. Clarke adds that no character was meaner in Jewish eyes and reports from Herodotus that Egyptian swineherds were barred from society, from worship and from marriage. Robertson calls it an unspeakable degradation, Theophylact assigns the work to those who outdid others in vice and taught their trade to others, and Ellicott reads it inwardly as a state in which a man’s whole energy serves his baser appetites.

The food is a small crux of its own. Clarke argues from a botanist that the Greek word does not mean husks at all, the botanical writers using another term, and that it denotes the fruit of the carob tree common in Syria, used as swine feed. Barnes quotes a traveller on fleshy pods lined with a gelatinous substance not unpleasant when ripe, seen in Cypriot orchards and still fed to swine, and notes the tree is called Saint John’s Bread from a mistaken idea about the Baptist’s diet. Robertson derives the word as a diminutive of the word for horn, from the shape of the pods. Ellicott records that many of the best manuscripts read simply desired to be satisfied rather than the coarser phrase, and suggests the variation may go back to Luke himself. Gill produces a rabbinic tale of a teacher hidden in a cave for whom a carob tree and a spring were created. Barnes and Robertson agree on the sting in the last clause: the refusal was continuous, and even the swine’s ration was measured out and not his to take.
17:
The phrase came to himself is treated by nearly everyone as clinical. Barnes points out that it is what we say of a man recovered from derangement, and takes the folly for a kind of insanity, quoting Ecclesiastes on the madness in men’s hearts; Clarke agrees and calls repentance a restoration to sound sense. Gill spreads it over two types: the voluptuary who promises himself liberty while a slave, and the self-righteous man who prides himself on rags while a robe is offered. Robertson keeps it spatial — he had been as far from himself as from home — and reads the Greek word by word, the father’s house surrounded by loaves as by a flood while I on the other hand am here perishing; Clarke notes that many witnesses add that here. Ellicott finds another suggestion in it: the guilt was self-indulgence, but the self he lived to was not his true self, so repentance begins by waking as from an evil dream.

Ambrose puts it as a paradox: a man returns to himself because he had departed from himself, since whoever returns to God restores himself to himself. Augustine locates the turn as the moment a mind is brought back from what entices it outwardly into the recesses of conscience. Gregory of Nyssa marks the arc plainly: the son who had despised his father came back chastened, broken by hardship and by eating with the swine. Chrysostom hears wounded rank. The young man became sensible of what had ruined him, having thrown himself by his own will from his father to strangers, from home to exile, from abundance to famine; and the cry means, I am no stranger but the son of a good father, and I who am free and noble have sunk below the hired men.

Those hired men draw out a set of distinctions. Ellicott identifies them as men who serve God from hope of reward rather than filial love, and finds that even in that lower duty they get what satisfies them, so the son who threw away his sonship envies servants beneath him. Basil sorts obedience into three kinds: the servile, which avoids evil for fear of punishment; the mercenary, which obeys for the wage; and the filial, which obeys for the good itself and out of love for the lawgiver. Ambrose says the son who holds the pledge of the Spirit keeps an heir’s right rather than seeking a wage, and that these servants abound not in husks but in bread. Augustine sharpens the mercenaries into preachers who handle the same bread of the word in the same house and preach no false gospel, yet hire themselves for a temporal reward. Bede reads the calculation the other way: the son does not claim a son’s affection but asks a hireling’s place, and admits even that he could not deserve unapproved. Barnes keeps the class in view as men born to nothing with no friends to provide for them, and hears the sting of the last words — I, who had property and a kind father.

Calvin turns from the son to the method. Hunger, he says, proved the best teacher; if men were wise of their own accord God would draw them gently, but since they will not stoop until subdued by the rod he applies hard wedges to hard knots, and every misery we endure is a profitable invitation to repentance. He adds a condition the others leave out: no punishment would have softened him without some prospect of advantage, so confidence in his father’s kindness gave the courage, and repentance must begin in an acknowledgment of mercy sufficient to raise hope. Henry calls this the turning point of conversion, where the Lord opens a man’s eyes, he sees every object differently, and perceives that the meanest servant of God is happier than he is.
18:
Robertson reads the decision as an act of will following the recovery of sight, and notes that the hard word is the one he says first — a verb meaning to miss the mark, set against the high-handed demand of the opening. Ellicott presses the tense, I sinned, a look back to the first act as containing all that grew from it, and calls the resolve the firstfruits of repentance: he remembers he has a father and trusts that love, but dares not claim the place he threw away. The first impulse of a contrite heart, he adds, is to take the lowest place and ask for the drudgery of daily duties, if only it may be near its Father and slowly regain his favour. Wesley marks the same thing without ornament: how accurately the first steps of true repentance are set out here.

Barnes reads the opening verb as a Hebrew idiom for setting about a piece of business rather than a change of posture, and draws the moral hard. The son goes to the very father he has dishonoured, because there is nowhere else to go and no other arm is strong enough to deliver from sin; and though a man cannot approach one he has wronged except with shame, unless he will go and confess he can never be saved. Gill traces a further stage in the resolution. The man had already left his harlots and his old course of living while still in the same country, which a man may do and remain unregenerate; what is new is that he means to leave the country itself, quit the fields and the ministry he had attached himself to, and abandon the swine and the husks together.

The phrase against heaven is where the readings part. Barnes takes heaven as a plain substitute for God and makes the recognition that sin is chiefly against God the mark of genuine repentance, citing the confession of David, who after the deepest injuries to men still said that he had sinned against God only; the offence against the father remains real, in wasted property and neglected counsel, and a true penitent will acknowledge wrongs to men as readily as wrongs to God. Wesley agrees in a line that heaven here means God. Clarke agrees that the Jews used the periphrasis to avoid pronouncing the divine name, but reports a rival construal — that the words should be rendered even unto heaven, a Hebrew idiom meaning that the man had sinned exceedingly, beyond all description.

Three older readings go elsewhere. Chrysostom proposes that heaven may here stand for Christ, arguing that to sin against heaven, which is above us but still a visible element, is the same as to sin against the manhood the Son of God took into himself for our salvation. Augustine raises the question whether the two clauses name one thing or two, and suggests that heaven may be the father’s own supremacy, or else that the sin was against heaven in the sight of the souls of the saints and before the father in the sanctuary of conscience. Ambrose reads it as the heavenly gifts of the Spirit spoiled by the soul’s sin, or as the bosom of the mother Jerusalem which is above and which a man ought never to leave. He also turns the confession into counsel: though God knows all things he waits for the voice of confession, since the man who throws the weight on himself lightens the load of his error and forestalls his accuser; there is no hiding from one whom nothing escapes, and it is safe to disclose what is already known. Bede notes that the request that follows is pitched below sonship on purpose — the man asks a servant’s wage and admits that even this depends on his father’s approval.
19:
Robertson calls the disclaimer a confession of the facts: the hired servants in his father’s house now stand high above him. Gill takes the renunciation to cover national adoption too, so that a man who once valued himself on being called a son owns his unworthiness in any sense. Barnes reads the request as humility, love for his father’s house and confidence of kind treatment even as a servant — but also as an inadequate sense of his father’s character, since the son asked far less than he received, as every sinner undervalues God and finds him more merciful than he dared hope.

The execution follows at once. Wesley notes that the moment he resolved he began to carry it out, and Robertson finds the same promptness in the Greek, with a genitive absolute showing the father watching at that very moment and so already looking for him. Gill argues that the resolve was of grace because it was executed: the man did not confer with flesh and blood nor stop at the distance, the danger or the cold reception he might expect, but quitted the far country, the citizen, the swine and the husks, denying sinful and righteous self together. Barnes reads the pace as deliberate contrast: no haste on the son’s side, only a man driven by want, filled with shame and doubting his welcome — the son came slowly, the father ran. He finds the point of the parable here, since not even a Pharisee could blame such a father. Clarke and Robertson agree on the compound verb: he kissed him again and again. Ellicott dresses the man in the story’s own terms, weary, footsore and in rags, and in the interpretation as one poor in spirit with feeble knees, needing more than rags of his own to cover him, still a great way off and there met by the love that answers to the kiss.

Calvin makes this the main point of the parable and then turns it into an argument. If men prone to revenge and tenacious of their rights can be moved by fatherly love to forgive and restore, God, whose goodness exceeds the affection of all the fathers in the world, will not be harsher; nothing is attributed to this father that God does not promise of himself, as when he answers before we call, or when David’s purpose to confess was met by forgiveness. So the father meets his son before hearing a word and embraces him filthy as he is. Against this Calvin sets what he calls wretched sophistry: the inference that grace is not shown to sinners until they anticipate it by repenting, so that God bestows nothing except on those who first begin to seek him. He grants that grief of conscience is required for pardon, but denies that repentance, itself God’s gift, arises from a man’s own motion, since no earthly father can renew a stubborn heart as God turns stone into flesh.

The older readings dwell on the running. Chrysostom asks what else it can mean than that our sins prevent us reaching God by our own strength, so that God, who can come to the weak, comes; and the mouth is kissed because from it came the confession that rose from the heart. Ambrose has the father hear the heart’s secrets within and run out lest anyone stop him — foreknowledge in the running, mercy in the embrace — falling on the neck to lift a man bent to earth under his sins; he would rather be a son than a sheep, since the sheep is found by the shepherd but the son honoured by the father. Augustine makes the neck the place where the Father lowers his own Arm, which is Christ, in whom he has always been running after our wanderings. Gregory of Nyssa says the meditated confession alone won the father over.
21:
Ellicott finds power in the exact repetition, since a contrite soul does not vary its phrasing, but finds more in what is missing: having seen his father, the son cannot ask again for a hireling’s place, a wish right before and now savouring of unreality. Penitents behave so, standing far off at first and hardly daring to hope for sonship, then unable to be satisfied with less once they have felt the kiss. Augustine had said as much — the man who wanted to be a hired servant while he had no bread nobly disdained the request after the kiss. The text is unsettled here. Clarke reports that several manuscripts add the clause and judges it an interpolation made to square the speech with the earlier resolve, losing a great beauty, since the point is a father cutting short a tale of self-reproach. Robertson agrees the son may not have finished, but notes the leading early manuscripts carry the words and thinks the father interrupted. Wesley draws the moral: so does God frequently cut an earnest confession short by a display of pardoning love, and Gill has the son prevented from asking pardon at all by the kiss already given.

Calvin uses the confession to define a second branch of repentance, conviction attended by grief and shame, since a man who is not grieved will attempt anything sooner than return to duty. He presses the earlier phrase about coming to oneself as showing a man whose wild desires had hurried him into forgetfulness of himself, which is why Scripture commands transgressors to return to their heart. The confession he distinguishes sharply from the auricular kind he says the papacy contrived: this one simply appeases an offended father, and sinning against heaven and before him means God was offended in the person of an earthly parent, since whoever rebels against the parent God set over him rebels against God.

Chrysostom notices that the father answers nobody: he speaks to his steward rather than his son, because a penitent who prays receives no reply in words yet sees mercy at work. Gill hears the same generosity in the conjunction, that though the son called himself unworthy the father would hear nothing of it. Robertson takes the robe as a stately garment reaching to the feet and insists first means first in rank, not first to hand, the finest in the house against the son’s rags; sandals and ring are marks of a freeman, slaves going barefoot. Clarke makes it the festal garment laid by for high days, like the one kept for Esau and used to disguise Jacob, adds instances of the ring as a mark of dignity, and recalls that captives lost their shoes and had them restored with liberty.

Whether to read the three gifts symbolically is itself disputed. Barnes refuses: the images fill out the narrative and press the one truth that God treats returning penitents with kindness, and should not be spiritualised. Calvin holds it idle to follow out every circumstance, but allows that the Father buries our sins and restores the gifts we were stripped of, having taken them away to shame our ingratitude. Ellicott concedes the caution and then does the work anyway, since here the symbolism lies near the surface: the robe is the garment of praise; the ring is the signet on the right hand, the seal of calling and election; the shoes answer to the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace, which a man need not put off even on holy ground. Augustine makes the robe the dignity Adam lost and the servants the preachers of reconciliation; Ambrose calls it the cloak of wisdom and the ring the seal of unfeigned faith, Bede reading the hand as a man’s working; Theophylact takes the servants for ministering spirits, or priests who clothe the soul with Christ in baptism.
23:
Whether the killing of the calf is a sacrifice is disputed, and the disagreement is flat. Clarke translates the imperative as sacrifice it and explains that animals provided for public feasts were in ancient times first offered to God, the blood poured out by way of atonement and the flesh thereby consecrated, so that the guests were held to be feeding on divine food — a custom he says is still kept in the East. Ellicott agrees at least that the word is the technical one for slaying a victim, and finds in it a half-suggestion that the joy was possible only through a death; he adds that the definite article points to the calf, one already fattened for some particular feast, answering to the feast of fat things promised by Isaiah, and that the whole detail comes to stand for what the eucharistic feast is a symbol, a witness and a pledge of. He also recalls that a second-century teacher took this passage as an illustration of the priestly emphasis he found characteristic of this Gospel. Robertson refuses the whole line in five words: the calf is killed not as a sacrifice but for the feast. He keeps to the vocabulary instead — the adjective means fed on wheat, and the animal was kept fat against festive occasions, possibly in the hope of this very return. Gill takes the calf for Christ outright, in allusion to the calves offered as sin offerings, peace offerings and burnt offerings on the day of atonement, and alternatively as the best provision a believer can feed on.

The call to be merry is corrected by two voices at once. Barnes says the English does not render the Greek: merriment suggests a light, playful, jovial mirth, whereas the word means simply joy, and the phrase is literally eating, let us rejoice. Wesley makes the same point from the other end, that wherever the word occurs in either Testament it implies nothing of levity but a solid, serious, religious, heartfelt joy, which was the ordinary sense of the English word two hundred years before he wrote.

On the father’s reason the readings differ in degree rather than kind. Barnes allows two senses for was dead — that the father had supposed him dead and now knows otherwise, or that he was dead to virtue, sunk in vice — and prefers the second, noting that Scripture regularly speaks of restoration to virtue as a return to life. Clarke agrees and adds that the figurative use is good Greek, found in the best writers. Gill takes it further into doctrine, listing death in Adam, death in law under sentence of condemnation, and death in trespasses and sins, which he unfolds as separation from God, loss of original righteousness, darkened understanding and a stubborn will. Ellicott stays with the story first — absence, alienation and self-chosen shame had made the father think of his son as dead, and death would have been easier to bear — then reads repentance as a passing from the death of sin to the life of righteousness. He also notices the structural point: lost and found are the words that link this parable to the two before it and complete the trilogy. Robertson glosses the verb as living again and calls the passive was found timeless, a man found at last after long waiting.
25:
Bede sets the third parable apart: the first two hinted at the joy Christ shares with the angels over penitents, while this one also blames the murmuring of the envious. On whom the elder son stands for the readers divide. Barnes and Wesley take him plainly for the Pharisees who had found fault. Gill argues by elimination — not angels, not mature converts, who are not ignorant of spiritual mirth and do not resent conversions or boast so, and not the Jews against the Gentiles — leaving the scribes and Pharisees against the publicans. Calvin allows that those who read the Jewish nation have some argument on their side but says they do not attend to the whole passage, since the discourse was occasioned by the scribes; and he notes that Christ concedes them their pretended holiness for the sake of argument, as if to say that even were the boast true they still ought not to reject repentant brethren so cruelly. Henry holds both, taking the character for the Pharisees though not of them alone, and finds God’s grace shining almost as bright in his gentle bearing with peevish saints as in his receiving of prodigals. Augustine reads Israel outright — not in a far country but not in the house either, out in the field of the Law and the Prophets, working at earthly things — and takes the father’s going out as a promise that when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in there will be an open calling of the Jews. Ambrose agrees, the younger son being the Gentile people envied by Israel, and adds that the elder is so called because a man grows old quickly through envy, and stands outside because his malice shuts him out. Theophylact offers a wider reading, the complainer standing for everyone offended at the sudden salvation of others, as in the psalm where a man takes offence at the peace of sinners.

The kid provokes an argument the sources conduct among themselves. Ambrose contrasts the kid the Jew asks for with the lamb the Christian receives, notes that Barabbas was released to them while a lamb was sacrificed for us, and suggests that those who seek a kid are waiting for Antichrist. Augustine rejects that reading outright: it is absurd that a son told thou art ever with me should be asking for belief in Antichrist; the elder son cannot be limited to such Jews as would believe in him; and one who did not believe in him could hardly feast on him. His own answer is that the Lord himself was what the son was denied, since a nation reckoning Christ a sabbath-breaker treats him as a kid rather than a lamb. Jerome proposes instead that no blood of prophet or priest ever delivered the nation from Roman power, and Theophylact that the kid is a persecuting sinner whose fall the sufferer might have enjoyed, as Ahab was to Elijah. Jerome adds the deeper answer, that all justice compared with God’s is injustice.

The music divides the philologists. Ellicott identifies a symphony, a concert implying voices as well as instruments, found nowhere else in the New Testament though present in the Greek of Daniel, and takes the second word as the one used of the chorus of Greek drama, from which our word choir descends, so that singing is probably included. Clarke goes further, reporting a scholar who denies that the word means dancing at all, since it properly denotes a choir of singers. Robertson keeps the dance and makes it concrete: a circular dance on the green. Barnes assumes dancing and turns aside to defend the mention of it, citing Miriam and David, insisting that our Lord expresses no opinion on its propriety and that mentioning it pleads for its lawfulness no more than mentioning the younger son’s vices justifies them.
26:
The exchange is brief and the commentators mostly work on its wording. Robertson notes that the word for the servant questioned is not the one used a few verses earlier for the bondslaves who fetched the robe; the Greeks used this term loosely, so the man could be either a hired servant or a slave. The verb for the questioning is an imperfect middle, which he takes to mean the elder son asked repeatedly and eagerly, and he defends the construction that follows against a scholar who called it poor Greek, explaining that the form of the direct question has simply been kept in the indirect, as it is elsewhere in Luke and in Acts.

Gill gives the detail a motive. It is characteristic, he says, of the men this son represents that he asks a servant rather than his father, exactly as the scribes and Pharisees preferred to put their objections to one of the disciples rather than to Christ himself. He also records that the versions vary at the opening of the answer, some dropping the connective and one making the servants answer in the plural.

Augustine reads the consultation as an act of reading. The servant called aside is a prophet taken up and searched, so that the elder son is asking, in effect, why these feasts are being kept in the church he finds himself standing next to; and the father’s servant, the prophet, gives him his answer. In that answer he hears the reason for the greater rejoicing — the brother had been in the farthest parts of the earth, and it is from the end of the earth that the new song rises.

On the servant’s report the notes are lexical. Robertson works through three tenses that English cannot easily match: the verb for is come is a present with perfect force, the verb for the killing is a plain past, and the verb for receiving carries a prefix meaning back, so the sense is that the father has got him back. The last word he renders as being in good health, and adds the sting: in spite of everything the young man has been through, and in spite of the father’s fears. Ellicott gives the same word as literally in health and observes that the participle is one he has marked before as characteristic of Luke and of Paul. Wesley notices which detail the servant chose to report, and guesses that the killing of the calf was mentioned rather than the robe or the ring because it stood nearer to the music and dancing the elder son had just heard.
28:
Robertson reads the anger as an eruption: an ingressive aorist, so that the man flew into a rage, the explosion of a long resentment and of a settled suspicion that his father favoured the wayward son. The refusal to go in is an imperfect, a standing unwillingness, and the entreaty another imperfect — the father kept on beseeching him. Ellicott puts the irony in a sentence: the son who professed obedience is out of harmony with his father’s mind, shuts love out, and by a just judgment finds himself shut out from love. Wesley admits how natural the resentment is. Gill translates the offence into doctrine, taking the killed calf for the preaching of a crucified Christ, and lists what galls self-righteous men in it — that salvation should be free, discriminating, complete and for sinners, when they would prefer a Christ who gave rules for saving ourselves or saved by example.

Whether the complaint has any justice at all is pressed from several sides. Clarke calls the anger improper on every view, since the father had divided his whole substance and this son had already received his portion, which he might have taken away whenever he chose; whatever the father acquired afterwards was his to dispose of, and by the eastern law Clarke cites the other children could claim no share in such a gift. Barnes makes the same point more shortly and adds that the father had always treated him kindly. Calvin goes further and grants the premise for argument’s sake: even if a man had discharged every duty of piety perfectly, even were he not inferior in holiness to the angels, he would still have no just cause to complain that his brother is pardoned. He reads the father’s coming out as a reproach to the pride of hypocrites, and notes that though God does not entreat us, by this example he exhorts us to bear with our brethren’s faults. Theophylact makes the same concession as a question: grant that you are truly just and have transgressed nothing — must we for that reason refuse those who turn from their iniquities? Chrysostom asks whether grief at another’s prosperity is simply envy and answers that no saint grieves at such things, but counts the good of others his own.

The boast itself is dissected. Ellicott fastens on the verb: it means to serve as a slave serves, so the obedience had all along been servile, prompted by fear and hope; and the men it portrays are conscious of no transgressions, which is precisely why they have no joy in forgiveness and no power to share anyone else’s. Robertson finds the same slavery in the word and suspects a man who stayed at home while longing to follow his brother, and he sets the tenses against each other — not once did he transgress, against so many years of serving. Wesley draws a conclusion the others avoid: this man is one of the instances the earlier verse spoke of, so that the parable confirms it, and he adds that God does not usually give much joy to those who never felt the sorrows of repentance. Augustine limits the claim rather than granting it, taking the unbroken commandment to be not every precept but the essential one of worshipping no other God, so that the son stands for those Israelites who never turned to idols.
30: Everyone hears contempt in the last speech. Barnes calls this thy son an expression of great contempt, since he will not say my brother but names him as his father’s, insulting both at once; never, he says, was there a more striking instance of petty malice. Clarke agrees that the man would not condescend to use his brother’s name or to acknowledge the relation, and finds him bitterly reproaching an affectionate father in the same breath. Ellicott watches discontent pass into scorn and bitterness, the wanderer’s sin painted at once in the coarsest and darkest colours, and hears a concentrated malignity in the very turn of the phrase. Gill hears in the refusal of the word brother a man who will not own the relation the father has just acknowledged, and reads the whole objection as offence that a crucified Christ should be preached to sinners at all, still less so soon — as though the penitent ought first to be sent away to cleanse himself, or to get some peace of his own, before applying for a cure his case needs at once. Robertson catches what is not said: he does not say this my brother, and the verb is neither came back nor came home but a bare arrival. The word for devouring is literally eaten down, a perfective the feasting itself suggested. And the charge about harlots, though the narrative bears it out, is something the elder son cannot have known; Robertson suspects it reflects what the accuser would have done in the same case. Jerome had already said as much, that this shameless son resembles the Pharisee justifying himself, keeping the law in the letter and accusing his brother wickedly, while Augustine reads the harlots as the superstitions of the Gentiles, a soul that has left the true marriage of the true God going after evil spirits. Ambrose turns it on the reader: those who seem righteous to themselves are angry when pardon is granted to a man confessing his sins, and we ought to favour forgiveness after repentance, lest in grudging it to another we fail to obtain it ourselves — we too were once far off.
31:
Robertson notes that the word the father uses is not the formal one but simply child, and that the pronoun is expressed and placed emphatically: thou art ever with me — a man who had never appreciated his privileges at home. Calvin sets the answer out as two arguments. The first is that the elder son has no cause for anger, since his brother’s reception costs him nothing: though he has carried nothing out of the house, his rights are preserved undiminished and his condition is not the worse. The second is that, without any regard for his brother’s safety, he is grieved at the rejoicing that safety occasioned, when he ought to have shared it. Both points, Calvin says, deserve attention, since we lose nothing when God receives into favour those who were at variance with him, and it is wicked hardness of heart not to rejoice at seeing our brethren drawn out of death.

Wesley draws the same conclusion for the murmurer’s comfort and then withdraws half of it: the father’s receiving the younger son did not disinherit the elder, so God’s receiving notorious sinners is no loss to those who have always served him — but neither will he raise the returning sinner to a glory equal to theirs, if on the whole they have made greater progress in inward as well as outward holiness. Ellicott asks whether the compliment is ironical, spoken from the Pharisees’ own valuation of themselves, and answers that it need not be taken so. The words were literally true of them and of Israel: the covenants, the law, the promises, the ordinances of worship and the teaching of wise men had all in fact been given, as like blessings are offered now to every member of the visible church. What was lacking was only the power to use them as the Father wills, and so to enjoy them. Gill grants the title in the same way, that he was a son by creation, by national adoption and by profession. Barnes settles the legal question underneath the complaint: the property had been divided, so what remained was in reality the elder son’s, he was heir to all of it and might have used it if he chose, and he therefore had no ground of complaint at all.
32:
Ellicott presses the Greek of the closing verse: it expresses moral necessity rather than fitness — we must needs rejoice, it could not be otherwise — and finds the repetition of he was dead singularly emphatic, since that and nothing else was the true account of what had happened, and it ought to be a source of joy to all the man’s kindred. He also hears tenderness as well as reproof in the way the scornful this thy son is answered by this thy brother, a fact the elder son had forgotten while almost disclaiming his own sonship. Wesley makes the same observation and calls it one of a thousand delicate touches that escape an inattentive reader, drawing from it the amazing intimation that the best of men ought to account the worst sinners their brethren still, and to remember the relation especially when such men show any inclination to return. Clarke reads it as the father returning the son’s own unkind words in a wholly different spirit: this son of mine to whom I show mercy is thy brother, and he is no longer the man he was. Robertson finds the necessity in the father’s heart rather than in propriety, and notes that the two verbs mean deep-seated joy and not mere hilarity, the father simply repeating to his elder son what he had already said to his servants.

Barnes and Clarke both close by stating the parable’s purpose, and both make the same forensic point. Barnes says it was designed to vindicate the receiving of sinners and to show the objectors’ conduct unreasonable, and that it had the designed effect of silencing them. He draws out a series of lessons — that a sinner’s disposition is selfish and impatient of delay, that sinners waste their blessings into want and wretchedness, that they disregard the woes to come, and that affliction is often what brings them to reflection, since men think little about God while their mercies last. Clarke argues that the hearers, unable to approve the elder son or condemn the father, were forced to justify Christ’s reception of tax-gatherers and to condemn themselves at least in the silence of their hearts. Gill adds that the elder brother himself had reason to keep the feast, had he felt for his kinsmen what the apostle felt for his. Robertson ends where the parable does, with the objectors put to silence by a picture of their own attitude.
